blocks.instruction: Choose TWO letters, A–E, for each question.

people.name: Nikhil Barrantes
people.role: supply-chain consultant who describes the 'two-speed system'

people.name: Valeria Ostrowski
people.role: labour economist who interviewed garment workers about overtime

people.name: Joana Hatfield
people.role: retail analyst who studied the purchases of resale app users

paragraphs.text: For most of the twentieth century, the clothing trade ran to a slow and predictable calendar. Collections were planned as much as a year ahead, manufactured in large volumes and delivered to shops twice a year, once for spring and summer and once for autumn and winter. Retailers had to guess what customers would want long before anyone wore it, and when they guessed wrongly, unsold stock was cleared through end-of-season sales. Fast fashion overturned this arrangement. Its leading companies now introduce new lines every week, and some online sellers list thousands of new designs a day. As a result, clothing has become much cheaper relative to most other goods, while the number of garments the average shopper buys has risen sharply.
paragraphs.label: A

paragraphs.text: The method behind this speed is less about sewing faster than about deciding later. A typical cycle begins with observation: design teams study catwalk shows, street style and social media, looking for colours and shapes that are attracting attention. Rather than inventing styles of their own, they adapt existing ones, producing simplified versions that can be made cheaply. A small initial batch, sometimes only a few hundred pieces, is then manufactured and sent to selected stores or listed online. After that, sales figures are monitored hourly; items that sell quickly are reordered within days, while those that fail are withdrawn before much money has been lost. Because the company commits to large quantities only once demand has been demonstrated, it largely escapes the heavy discounting that once ate into retailers' profits.
paragraphs.label: B

paragraphs.text: Speed of this kind depends on geography as much as on information. Many fast-fashion firms keep part of their production close to their main markets. For European retailers, that often means factories in Turkey, Morocco or Eastern Europe, where wages are higher than in South Asia but finished goods can arrive by lorry within a week instead of spending a month at sea. Basic items such as plain T-shirts, socks and underwear, for which demand changes little from year to year, are still made in large volumes in countries such as Bangladesh and Vietnam. Nikhil Barrantes, a supply-chain consultant, describes this as a 'two-speed system': companies pay extra for flexibility on trend-led products and squeeze costs on everything else.
paragraphs.label: C

paragraphs.text: The pressure to be both cheap and quick does not disappear; it is passed down the chain to factories. Brands typically negotiate a fixed price per garment and may alter quantities or designs at short notice, and suppliers who fear losing contracts rarely refuse. Valeria Ostrowski, a labour economist, interviewed around 300 garment workers in two exporting countries and concluded that last-minute changes to orders were more closely linked to unpaid overtime than the low prices paid per item. In her view, the problem lies as much in the buying practices of brands as in the wages set by factory owners. Safety is a further concern. In 2013, the collapse of a factory building near Dhaka, Bangladesh, killed more than a thousand garment workers and led to a legally binding agreement under which many international brands committed to supporting independent safety inspections.
paragraphs.label: D

paragraphs.text: The environmental bill is just as large. Growing cotton requires vast quantities of water, and dyeing and finishing fabric release chemicals that, where regulation is weak, often end up in rivers. Polyester, now the most widely used fibre, is made from oil and sheds tiny plastic fibres whenever it is washed. Perhaps the most striking change, however, concerns how clothes are used rather than how they are made. Research suggests that the average garment is now worn considerably fewer times before being thrown away than at the start of this century, and only a tiny fraction of discarded clothing is recycled into new garments. Much of the rest is buried or burned, while bales of second-hand clothing are shipped to markets in countries such as Ghana and Kenya, where traders report that a growing share is too worn or poorly made to sell.
paragraphs.label: E

paragraphs.text: Economists have a name for costs of this kind: externalities. These are costs that fall on people outside a transaction, such as communities living downstream of a dye works or workers whose health suffers, and they are not reflected in the price the shopper pays. When harmful effects are left out of prices, markets tend to produce more of a product than society would choose if it saw the full picture. One response is extended producer responsibility, under which companies contribute to the cost of collecting and recycling what they sell. France has applied such a scheme to clothing since 2007, and the European Union is moving towards similar rules.
paragraphs.label: F

paragraphs.text: Whether shoppers will change their habits is less certain. Resale and rental services have grown quickly, and many consumers tell surveys that sustainability matters to them. Yet a study by retail analyst Joana Hatfield, which tracked the purchases of 2,000 online customers, found that those who regularly sold clothes through resale apps bought more new items, not fewer, apparently because the prospect of reselling made each purchase feel less costly. If her findings hold, good intentions alone may not slow the cycle; what may matter more is whether prices begin to reflect the true costs of production.
paragraphs.label: G

section.text:
The True Cost of Cheap Clothes

A. For most of the twentieth century, the clothing trade ran to a slow and predictable calendar. Collections were planned as much as a year ahead, manufactured in large volumes and delivered to shops twice a year, once for spring and summer and once for autumn and winter. Retailers had to guess what customers would want long before anyone wore it, and when they guessed wrongly, unsold stock was cleared through end-of-season sales. Fast fashion overturned this arrangement. Its leading companies now introduce new lines every week, and some online sellers list thousands of new designs a day. As a result, clothing has become much cheaper relative to most other goods, while the number of garments the average shopper buys has risen sharply.

B. The method behind this speed is less about sewing faster than about deciding later. A typical cycle begins with observation: design teams study catwalk shows, street style and social media, looking for colours and shapes that are attracting attention. Rather than inventing styles of their own, they adapt existing ones, producing simplified versions that can be made cheaply. A small initial batch, sometimes only a few hundred pieces, is then manufactured and sent to selected stores or listed online. After that, sales figures are monitored hourly; items that sell quickly are reordered within days, while those that fail are withdrawn before much money has been lost. Because the company commits to large quantities only once demand has been demonstrated, it largely escapes the heavy discounting that once ate into retailers' profits.

C. Speed of this kind depends on geography as much as on information. Many fast-fashion firms keep part of their production close to their main markets. For European retailers, that often means factories in Turkey, Morocco or Eastern Europe, where wages are higher than in South Asia but finished goods can arrive by lorry within a week instead of spending a month at sea. Basic items such as plain T-shirts, socks and underwear, for which demand changes little from year to year, are still made in large volumes in countries such as Bangladesh and Vietnam. Nikhil Barrantes, a supply-chain consultant, describes this as a 'two-speed system': companies pay extra for flexibility on trend-led products and squeeze costs on everything else.

D. The pressure to be both cheap and quick does not disappear; it is passed down the chain to factories. Brands typically negotiate a fixed price per garment and may alter quantities or designs at short notice, and suppliers who fear losing contracts rarely refuse. Valeria Ostrowski, a labour economist, interviewed around 300 garment workers in two exporting countries and concluded that last-minute changes to orders were more closely linked to unpaid overtime than the low prices paid per item. In her view, the problem lies as much in the buying practices of brands as in the wages set by factory owners. Safety is a further concern. In 2013, the collapse of a factory building near Dhaka, Bangladesh, killed more than a thousand garment workers and led to a legally binding agreement under which many international brands committed to supporting independent safety inspections.

E. The environmental bill is just as large. Growing cotton requires vast quantities of water, and dyeing and finishing fabric release chemicals that, where regulation is weak, often end up in rivers. Polyester, now the most widely used fibre, is made from oil and sheds tiny plastic fibres whenever it is washed. Perhaps the most striking change, however, concerns how clothes are used rather than how they are made. Research suggests that the average garment is now worn considerably fewer times before being thrown away than at the start of this century, and only a tiny fraction of discarded clothing is recycled into new garments. Much of the rest is buried or burned, while bales of second-hand clothing are shipped to markets in countries such as Ghana and Kenya, where traders report that a growing share is too worn or poorly made to sell.

F. Economists have a name for costs of this kind: externalities. These are costs that fall on people outside a transaction, such as communities living downstream of a dye works or workers whose health suffers, and they are not reflected in the price the shopper pays. When harmful effects are left out of prices, markets tend to produce more of a product than society would choose if it saw the full picture. One response is extended producer responsibility, under which companies contribute to the cost of collecting and recycling what they sell. France has applied such a scheme to clothing since 2007, and the European Union is moving towards similar rules.

G. Whether shoppers will change their habits is less certain. Resale and rental services have grown quickly, and many consumers tell surveys that sustainability matters to them. Yet a study by retail analyst Joana Hatfield, which tracked the purchases of 2,000 online customers, found that those who regularly sold clothes through resale apps bought more new items, not fewer, apparently because the prospect of reselling made each purchase feel less costly. If her findings hold, good intentions alone may not slow the cycle; what may matter more is whether prices begin to reflect the true costs of production.
